title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
In the previous post, we introduced Linear Programming (LP), where decision variables are continuous. This works well when the decision represents a divisible quantity, such as the amount of products to manufacture, electricity to generate, or goods to transport.
However, many real-world optimization problems involve discrete decisions rather than continuous quantities.
For example:

Should a new warehouse be built?
Which projects should receive funding?
Which employee should be assigned to a task?
What is the shortest route that visits every customer exactly once?

These decisions cannot take fractional values. A warehouse cannot be built halfway, an employee cannot perform \(0.4\) of a job, and a project cannot be selected \(1.7\) times.
If these problems were modeled using Linear Programming, the optimal solution might contain fractional values that are mathematically feasible but practically meaningless.
To model such problems, we require decision variables to take integer values. This leads to Integer Programming (IP).






Integer Programming is useful when the decision is indivisible. The decision variable must represent a whole number or a yes-or-no choice.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Integer vs. Binary Decision Variables
Integer decision variables generally fall into two categories.

General Integer Variables
Some decisions represent discrete quantities, where only whole numbers are meaningful.
Examples include:

Number of buses to purchase
Number of workers to hire
Number of machines to install

These variables satisfy
\[
x\in\mathbb{Z},
\]
where \(\mathbb{Z}\) denotes the set of integers.


Binary Variables
Many optimization problems involve yes-or-no decisions.
Examples include:

Should this warehouse be opened?
Should this project be selected?
Should worker \(i\) be assigned to job \(j\)?

These decisions are naturally modeled using binary variables,
\[
x\in\{0,1\},
\]
where

\(1\) indicates Yes or selected,
\(0\) indicates No or not selected.

Because binary variables are integers restricted to two possible values, Binary Integer Programming (BIP) is a special case of Integer Programming.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Knapsack Problem
The Knapsack Problem is one of the simplest and most important Integer Programming models.
Suppose we have a limited budget, capacity, or resource. We must decide which items to select in order to maximize total value without exceeding the limit.
The decision variable is
\[
x_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if item } i \text{ is selected},\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
A basic knapsack model is
\[
\max \sum_{i\in I} v_i x_i
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{i\in I} w_i x_i \le C,
\]
\[
x_i\in\{0,1\},
\qquad
\forall i\in I.
\]
where

\(v_i\) is the value of item \(i\),
\(w_i\) is the weight or resource requirement of item \(i\),
\(C\) is the total capacity.







The knapsack problem is about selection under a limit: choose the best combination of items without exceeding capacity.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Assignment Problem
The Assignment Problem is a special case of the transportation problem, but it is usually formulated as a binary Integer Programming problem.
In an assignment problem, each source has a supply of one unit and each destination has a demand of one unit. For example, each worker can be assigned to one job, and each job needs exactly one worker.
The decision variable is
\[
x_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if worker } i \text{ is assigned to job } j,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The objective is often to minimize assignment cost:
\[
\min \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J} c_{ij}x_{ij}.
\]
Each worker is assigned to exactly one job:
\[
\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1,
\qquad
\forall i\in I.
\]
Each job receives exactly one worker:
\[
\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1,
\qquad
\forall j\in J.
\]
Finally,
\[
x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\]






The assignment problem can be viewed as a transportation problem where every supply and every demand equals \(1\). The binary variable ensures that the assignment is either made or not made.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Set Covering Problem
The Set Covering Problem asks:

What is the minimum-cost collection of sets that covers all required elements?

A common example is facility coverage. Suppose we need to choose fire stations so that every neighborhood is covered by at least one station.
Let
\[
x_j=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if set } j \text{ is selected},\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The objective is
\[
\min \sum_{j\in J} c_jx_j.
\]
Each requirement must be covered at least once:
\[
\sum_{j\in J_i}x_j\ge 1,
\qquad
\forall i\in I.
\]
where \(J_i\) is the set of options that can cover requirement \(i\).






Set covering means at least one selected option must cover each requirement.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Set Partitioning Problem
The Set Partitioning Problem is similar to set covering, but it is stricter.
Instead of requiring each element to be covered at least once, set partitioning requires each element to be covered exactly once.
The model is
\[
\min \sum_{j\in J} c_jx_j
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j\in J_i}x_j=1,
\qquad
\forall i\in I,
\]
\[
x_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]






Set covering uses \(\ge 1\), while set partitioning uses \(=1\).

Set covering: every requirement must be covered at least once.
Set partitioning: every requirement must be covered exactly once.




Set partitioning is commonly used in problems such as airline crew scheduling, vehicle routing, and task assignment, where each flight, customer, or task must be assigned to exactly one feasible route or schedule.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Traveling Salesman Problem
The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) asks:

What is the shortest route that visits every city exactly once and returns to the starting city?

The TSP is a classic combinatorial optimization problem. It is not simply a shortest path problem, because the route must visit all cities exactly once before returning to the starting point.
Let
\[
x_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the route travels directly from city } i \text{ to city } j,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The objective is
\[
\min \sum_{i\in N}\sum_{j\in N} c_{ij}x_{ij},
\]
where \(c_{ij}\) is the distance or travel cost from city \(i\) to city \(j\).
Each city must be entered exactly once:
\[
\sum_{i\in N}x_{ij}=1,
\qquad
\forall j\in N.
\]
Each city must be left exactly once:
\[
\sum_{j\in N}x_{ij}=1,
\qquad
\forall i\in N.
\]
Additional constraints are needed to eliminate subtours, which are smaller disconnected cycles that do not visit every city in one complete tour.






The TSP is not the same as the shortest path problem. The shortest path problem finds the cheapest path from one node to another, while the TSP finds the cheapest tour that visits every node exactly once.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Scheduling Problems
Scheduling problems ask:

Which jobs should be performed, when should they be performed, and in what order?

Many scheduling problems are modeled as Integer Programming or Mixed Integer Programming problems because they involve discrete decisions.
For example,
\[
x_{it}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if job } i \text{ starts at time } t,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Scheduling can also be connected to set covering or set partitioning. For example, in workforce scheduling, each feasible work pattern can be treated as a set of shifts covered by one employee. The optimization then chooses a collection of work patterns so that all required shifts are covered.






Scheduling is an application area, while set covering and set partitioning are mathematical formulations. Some scheduling problems can be formulated as set covering or set partitioning problems.

title: Integer Programming: Optimizing Discrete Decisions
text:
Summary
Integer Programming is used when decision variables must represent whole numbers or yes-or-no choices. It is especially useful for problems involving selection, assignment, routing, facility location, and scheduling.







Model
Core Idea




Knapsack
Select the best items under a capacity limit


Assignment
Match resources to tasks one-to-one


Set Covering
Cover every requirement at least once


Set Partitioning
Cover every requirement exactly once


Traveling Salesman Problem
Find the shortest tour visiting every city once


Scheduling
Decide timing, ordering, or resource assignment



The main difference between LP and IP is not the objective function or constraint structure. Both can still be linear. The key difference is the domain of the decision variables.

LP allows continuous decision variables.
IP restricts some or all decision variables to integers.
Binary IP restricts variables to \(0\) or \(1\).

This makes Integer Programming especially powerful for modeling real-world decisions that are discrete, indivisible, or logical.

Network optimization is a special class of linear programming problems in which decisions are represented on a network consisting of nodes and arcs.

Nodes represent entities, such as factories, warehouses, customers, jobs, or workers.
Arcs represent the possible connections between nodes, such as transportation routes, communication links, or assignment decisions.

text:
2.1 Transportation Problem
A transportation problem is min cost flow problem with the following two properties:

It is defined on a complete bipartite graph, where the nodes are divided into two disjoint sets: sources and destinations. Every source can potentially ship directly to every destination, so every source–destination pair corresponds to a decision variable.
Arcs have costs but there are no upper bound on the flows. (Supply and demand naturally cap the flow.)


LP formulation
In a tabular representation, each row corresponds to a source, each column corresponds to a destination, and each cell contains the decision variable \(x_{ij}\), representing the quantity shipped from source \(i\) to destination \(j\).





The tableau provides an intuitive way to understand the constraints of the transportation problem before writing the mathematical model.
The objective is to minimize the total transportation cost.
\[
\min \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
where

\(c_{ij}\): unit transportation cost from source \(i\) to destination \(j\)
\(x_{ij}\): shipment quantity from source \(i\) to destination \(j\)



Supply Constraints
Each source has a limited amount of available supply. In the table, each row corresponds to a source. Summing across a row gives the total amount shipped from that source.
For example, the first row represents \(x_{11}+x_{12}+\cdots+x_{1n}\), which is the total shipment leaving source 1. \[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ij}=a_i,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]

Demand Constraits
Each destination has a required demand that must be satisfied.Similarly, each column corresponds to a destination. Summing down a column gives the total amount received by that destination.
For example, the first column represents \(x_{11}+x_{21}+\cdots+x_{m1}\), which is the total shipment arriving at destination 1.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_{ij}=b_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,n.
\]



Non-negativity Constraints
Negative shipment quantities are not physically meaningful. \[
x_{ij}\ge0,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,\;
j=1,\ldots,n
\]


Dummy Node

text:
2.2 Transshipment Problem
The transportation problem assumes that goods move directly from source nodes to destination nodes. However, in many real-world networks, goods may pass through intermediate facilities such as warehouses, ports, or distribution centers before reaching the final destination. This leads to the transshipment problem.
In a transshipment network, the decision variable $ x_{ij}$ represents the amount shipped from node \(i\) to node \(j\). For example, if goods move from node 1 to node 3 and then from node 3 to node 4, we write:
\[
x_{13}, \qquad x_{34}
\]
Here, node 3 appears as both the ending node of \(x_{13}\) and the starting node of \(x_{34}\). This means node 3 receives flow and then sends it onward.






NoteKey Idea



In a transshipment problem, intermediate nodes do not create or consume flow. They only transfer flow. Therefore, for every intermediate node:
\[
\text{Total inflow} = \text{Total outflow}
\]

href: posts/Common Applications of Linear Programming Problems (2).html#lp-formulation-1
title: What Is Linear Programming Used For? Common Applications and Examples in Network Programming
text:
LP Formulation
Let:

\(x_{ij}\) = flow shipped from node \(i\) to node \(j\)
\(c_{ij}\) = unit shipping cost from node \(i\) to node \(j\)
\(f\) = total amount of flow sent from the source to the sink

The objective is to minimize the cost:
\[
\min \sum_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]






Why does the objective function look different?
The transportation problem is defined on a complete bipartite graph, where the nodes are divided into two disjoint sets: sources and destinations. Every source can potentially ship directly to every destination, so every source–destination pair corresponds to a decision variable. Therefore, the objective sums over all pairs:
\[
\min \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J} c_{ij}x_{ij}.
\]
In a transshipment network, however, shipments can only travel along the existing arcs. Intermediate nodes are connected only to selected nodes rather than to every source or destination. As a result, the objective sums only over the set of arcs:
\[
\min \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}} c_{ij}x_{ij}.
\]









NoteUnderstanding the notation



The notation
\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A} x_{ij}
\]
means sum over all nodes \(j\) such that an arc \((i,j)\) exists.
In other words, it represents the total outgoing flow from node \(i\).
Similarly,
\[
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A} x_{ji}
\]
sums the flow over all arcs entering node \(i\), representing the total incoming flow.
This notation is used in general network models because, unlike the transportation problem, not every pair of nodes is directly connected by an arc.



Source Node
For convenience, assume the network contains \(n\) nodes, numbered from \(1\) to \(n\). Node \(1\) denotes the source, node \(n\) denotes the sink, and the remaining nodes may serve as intermediate nodes.
The source node is where the flow originates. It generates and sends flow into the network but does not receive flow from any other node. Therefore, the total flow leaving the source must equal the value of the flow, denoted by \(f\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{1j}=f.
\]
Equivalently, using the flow balance form,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{1j}-f=0.
\]


Intermediate Nodes
Intermediate nodes neither create nor consume flow. They simply transfer flow through the network. Therefore, for every intermediate node, the total inflow must equal the total outflow.
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ij}
-
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ji}
=0,
\qquad i=2,\ldots,n-1.
\]


Sink Node
Intermediate nodes only serve as transition points. They do not retain, create, or consume flow. Therefore, the total flow entering the sink must equal the value of the flow.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{in}=f.
\]
Equivalently, using the flow balance form,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{in}-f=0.
\]


Non-negativity Constraints
\[
x_{ij} \ge 0
\]
Flow cannot be negative.

text:
2.3 Minimum-Cost Flow (MCF)
The Minimum-Cost Flow (MCF) problem is the most general cost-based network optimization model. Both the transportation problem and the transshipment problem can be viewed as cases of the MCF problem.
In the transportation and transshipment problems, we must first identify the role of each node before formulating the LP model.

In a transportation problem, each node is classified as either a source or a destination (sink).
In a transshipment problem, each node is classified as a source, an intermediate node, or a sink.







The transportation and transshipment problems are both special cases of the Minimum-Cost Flow problem.

Transportation problem: A complete bipartite network with no intermediate nodes.
Transshipment problem: A general network with intermediate nodes.
Minimum-Cost Flow: A unified formulation in which every node satisfies the same flow balance equation.




The node type determines which flow balance equation is used.
The Minimum-Cost Flow (MCF) formulation takes a different approach. Instead of writing separate equations for different node types, it assigns every node a divergence (or net supply) denoted by \(b_i\).
If we define \(\text{Outflow} - \text{Inflow} = b_i\), then:



Divergence (\(b_i\))
Node Type
Interpretation




\(b_i > 0\)
Supply node
Generates flow into the network


\(b_i = 0\)
Intermediate node
Conserves flow (inflow = outflow)


\(b_i < 0\)
Demand node
Removes flow from the network



The objective is still to minimize the total transportation cost:
\[
\min \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}} c_{ij}x_{ij}.
\]
subject to the flow balance constraints
\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}} x_{ij}
-
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal{A}} x_{ji}
=
b_i,
\qquad
\forall i\in N,
\]
and the capacity constraints
\[
l_{ij}
\le
x_{ij}
\le
u_{ij},
\qquad
(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}.
\]
where

\(x_{ij}\): amount of flow sent along arc \((i,j)\).
\(c_{ij}\): unit transportation cost on arc \((i,j)\).
\(b_i\): divergence (net supply) at node \(i\).
\(l_{ij}\): lower capacity bound of arc \((i,j)\).
\(u_{ij}\): upper capacity bound of arc \((i,j)\).







The MCF formulation does not determine whether a node is a source, intermediate node, or sink. Those roles are still specified by the modeler through the values of \(b_i\). The advantage of MCF is that every node uses the same flow balance equation, making the formulation more compact and easier to generalize.

text:
2.4 Max Flow Problem
The maximum flow problem is not concerned with transportation cost. Instead, its goal is to determine the largest amount of flow that can be delivered from a source to a sink.
The key idea is that every arc in the network has a capacity, representing the maximum amount of flow that it can physically carry. The optimization seeks to maximize the total flow while ensuring that no arc exceeds its capacity.
For example, imagine a reservoir supplying water to a city.

The reservoir is the source node;
The households collectively represent the sink;
The pipes are the arcs connecting the network.

Although the reservoir may contain an abundant supply of water, each pipe has a limited diameter and can only carry a finite amount of water. These physical limitations are modeled by the capacity constraints on the arcs.
The maximum flow problem answers the following question:

Given the capacities of all pipes, what is the greatest amount of water that can be delivered from the reservoir to the households?

The capacity constraint for every arc is
\[
0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij},
\]
where

\(x_{ij}\) is the flow through arc \((i,j)\),
\(u_{ij}\) is the maximum capacity of arc \((i,j)\).

The maximum flow is a property of the entire network, not of any individual arc. It depends on how the network is connected and is often limited by one or more bottlenecks. For example:

Two parallel pipes with capacities 40 and 60 can jointly deliver 100 units of flow, even though neither individual pipe has capacity 100.
Two pipes connected in series with capacities 100 and 20 can deliver at most 20 units, because the smaller pipe becomes the bottleneck.

section: From Maximum Flow to Minimum-Cost Flow
text:
From Maximum Flow to Minimum-Cost Flow
The standard Maximum Flow problem seeks to maximize the total amount of flow delivered from the source to the sink,
\[
\max f.
\]
An equivalent formulation introduces a pseudo (artificial) return arc from the sink back to the source.
          Original Network

Source --------------------► Sink


      After Adding the Return Arc

        ┌────────────────────┐
        │                    │
        ▼                    │
Source --------------------► Sink
        ◄────────────────────
           Pseudo Return Arc
The return arc does not represent a physical connection. It is introduced purely for mathematical convenience.
Suppose the network delivers \(f\) units of flow from the source to the sink. The pseudo return arc simply returns those same \(f\) units back to the source. As a result, the network becomes a circulation, where no node creates or destroys flow.
Consequently, every node satisfies the same flow conservation equation,
\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}
-
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}
=
0,
\qquad
\forall i\in N.
\]
Furthermore, the flow on the return arc is exactly the total flow through the network,
\[
x_{ts}=f.
\]
Instead of maximizing \(f\), we can therefore maximize the flow on the return arc,
\[
\max x_{ts}.
\]






NoteWhy introduce the return arc?



The pseudo return arc is not required to solve the Maximum Flow problem.
Its purpose is to transform a source-to-sink flow problem into a circulation problem, allowing every node to satisfy the same flow balance equation. This provides a unified mathematical framework shared by many network flow models.



Connecting Maximum Flow to Minimum-Cost Flow
The Maximum Flow problem is a maximization problem,
\[
\max x_{ts},
\]
whereas the Minimum-Cost Flow (MCF) problem is formulated as
\[
\min \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A} c_{ij}x_{ij}.
\]
To express Maximum Flow as a special case of the MCF problem,

assign a cost of 0 to every original arc,
assign a cost of \(-1\) to the pseudo return arc.

The objective then becomes
\[
\min (-1)x_{ts}.
\]
Since minimizing \(-x_{ts}\) is equivalent to maximizing \(x_{ts}\),
\[
\min (-1)x_{ts}
\equiv
\max x_{ts}.
\]
Therefore, the Maximum Flow problem can be viewed as a special case of the Minimum-Cost Flow problem.






TipKey Insight



The pseudo return arc and the negative cost serve different purposes.

Pseudo return arc: transforms the network into a circulation, so every node satisfies the same flow conservation equation.
Negative unit cost: converts the maximization objective into the minimization objective used by the Minimum-Cost Flow formulation.

Together, they allow the Maximum Flow problem to be expressed within the unified Minimum-Cost Flow framework.

2.5 Assignment Problem
The Assignment Problem is a special case of the Transportation Problem.
Like the transportation problem, the network consists of only two layers of nodes:

a set of sources (e.g., workers, machines, or vehicles), and
a set of destinations (e.g., jobs, tasks, or projects).

There are no intermediate (transshipment) nodes, so the network remains a complete bipartite graph, where every source can potentially be assigned to every destination.
The key difference lies in the supply, demand, and decision variables.
In the transportation problem, a source may ship many units to multiple destinations. In contrast, the assignment problem assumes that each source can perform exactly one task, and each task must be assigned to exactly one source. Therefore,
\[
a_i = 1,
\qquad
\forall i,
\]
and
\[
b_j = 1,
\qquad
\forall j.
\]
The decision variable is defined as
\[
x_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if source } i \text{ is assigned to destination } j,\\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Since an assignment either occurs or does not occur, the decision variable must be binary,
\[
x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Consequently, the Assignment Problem is typically formulated as a Binary Integer Programming (BIP) problem, which is a special case of Integer Programming (IP).






TipRelationship to the Transportation Problem



The Assignment Problem can be viewed as a transportation problem in which every source has a supply of one unit and every destination has a demand of one unit. The additional binary constraint ensures that each source is assigned to exactly one destination and each destination receives exactly one assignment.

Looking Ahead
The transportation problem is the simplest network optimization model because goods move directly from sources to destinations.
More advanced network models extend this framework by introducing intermediate nodes or additional operational constraints.

Transshipment problem: allows intermediate warehouses or distribution centers.
Minimum-cost flow problem: allows arbitrary network structures.
Multi-period inventory networks: introduce storage and time.
Supply chain networks: combine production, transportation, and inventory decisions into one optimization model.

Although these models become more sophisticated, they all rely on the same underlying principle of flow conservation.

title: Why I Started This Optimization Blog
text:
When I first took Management Science at Carnegie Mellon University with Professor Holly Wiberg, I honestly had no idea what the subject was about. I assumed it would be something similar to business management or organizational strategy. Instead, I found myself learning about linear programming, duality, network optimization, and algorithms such as the simplex method.
Professor Wiberg is an incredibly thoughtful teacher: clear, patient, and genuinely supportive of her students. Although I was able to follow the lectures and complete the assignments, I often felt that I was understanding how to solve the problems without fully understanding why everything worked.
A year later, I had the opportunity to serve as a teaching assistant for Optimization for Decision Making, taught by Professor Peter Caulkins. Teaching the material forced me to revisit many concepts that I had only partially understood as a student. I also began reading books such as Introduction to Mathematical Programming and other optimization references, gradually filling in the gaps that had been left during my first exposure to the subject.
This blog is the result of that journey.
Its primary purpose is surprisingly selfish: it is my own notebook. Writing is the best way I know to organize ideas and remember concepts. Every post is an attempt to explain something that I once found confusing.
At the same time, I hope these articles are useful for readers who have little, or even no, background in optimization. If you have not studied mathematics for years, or have always been intimidated by mathematical notation, I hope this series shows that optimization is far more intuitive than it first appears.


Through my admittedly limited experience, I think optimization can be understood from two complementary perspectives.
The first is problem formulation.
This is the art of translating a real-world problem into mathematics. What are the decision variables? What exactly are we trying to optimize? Which constraints represent reality, and which are simplifying assumptions? How do we justify the model, and what are its limitations?
To me, this is the most creative part of optimization.
Unlike many machine learning problems, where we use historical data to predict future outcomes, optimization often begins with a blank sheet of paper. We first need to build a mathematical representation of reality before any algorithm can solve it. A well-formulated model is often more valuable than a sophisticated algorithm applied to the wrong problem.
The second perspective is the mathematics behind the algorithms.
Once the model has been formulated, another fascinating question emerges: How do we actually solve it?
This leads to beautiful ideas from linear algebra, geometry, graph theory, and computer science. Topics such as the simplex method, interior-point methods, branch-and-bound, network flow algorithms, and dynamic programming are not just computational tricks. They each reveal a different way of thinking about optimization.
This blog will gradually explore both perspectives.



I certainly think so.
Many optimization models are already embedded in our daily lives. They determine how airlines schedule aircraft, how package delivery routes are planned, how electricity is dispatched across power grids, how hospitals allocate resources, and how bike-sharing systems rebalance bicycles throughout a city.
Sometimes I even catch myself wondering:

Could optimization be applied to dating or matchmaking?

Whether the answer is yes or no is less interesting than the habit of thinking that optimization develops. Once you begin learning it, you start seeing decision problems everywhere.



What I enjoy most is not necessarily finding the optimal answer, but the process of building a model that captures an incredibly complicated world.
Reality is messy.
People are irrational. Information is incomplete. Objectives conflict with one another. Every model is an approximation.
Optimization constantly asks the same question:

How can we build a mathematical model that is simple enough to solve, yet realistic enough to be useful?

I find that question endlessly fascinating.
Perhaps surprisingly, this interest has also led me toward psychology and philosophy. Human decisions rarely follow perfect mathematical rules, yet mathematical models often provide remarkably useful approximations. Understanding where those approximations succeed, and where they fail, is just as interesting as the mathematics itself.
Another pleasant surprise was discovering that the mathematics itself is actually enjoyable.
Before coming to Carnegie Mellon, I had not seriously studied advanced mathematics for many years. At first, linear algebra and optimization notation looked almost like another language. But as I slowly worked through the ideas, they became much more intuitive than I had expected.
If someone like me can eventually make sense of these concepts, I hope others can as well.



Outside optimization, one of my favorite subjects is epistemology, the branch of philosophy that asks what knowledge is, how we know something is true, and how we distinguish good reasoning from bad reasoning.
In many ways, optimization feels connected to that pursuit.
Both disciplines ask us to start with assumptions, reason carefully, acknowledge limitations, and search for better answers rather than perfect ones.
Perhaps that is why I enjoy optimization so much.
It is not only about finding the best solution to a mathematical model.
It is also about learning how to think clearly in a world that is wonderfully, frustratingly, and beautifully complex.

title: Linear Programming: The Foundation of Optimization
text:
A function is linear if:

Variables only appear to the first power.

This means that:

Variables are not multiplied together.
Variables are not divided by each other.
No logarithms, exponentials, or trigonometric functions appear.



\[3x + 5y \le 100\]
\[\frac{1}{2}x + \frac{3}{4}y \le 20\]
\[2(x+y) \le 5\]



\[xy \le 100\] \[\frac{x}{y} \le 20\] \[\frac{1}{x} \le 3\] \[2xy + z \le 5\]




Many real-world decision problems can be approximated using linear relationships. For example, suppose a factory produces identical water bottles and earns $2 profit on each bottle sold. Producing 100 bottles generates $200 profit, while producing 200 bottles generates $400 profit. Each additional bottle increases profit by exactly $2, making the relationship linear.
Linear programming is attractive because it is:

Intuitive and easy to explain.
Often a reasonable approximation of more complex systems.

Of course, real-world systems are often more complicated than a linear programming model suggests. Once we introduce assumptions such as economies of scale, learning effects, nonlinear costs, or interactions between decisions, the relationship may no longer be linear. Nevertheless, linear programming provides a useful starting point and serves as the foundation for more advanced optimization methods.

title: Linear Programming: The Foundation of Optimization
text:
2.1 Decision Variables
DDecision variables represent the choices we can make, but whose values are unknown. The optimization model determines these values to optimize the objective while satisfying all constraints.
There is no single “correct” notation for decision variables. The notation should clearly reflect the decisions being modeled.

One-dimensional: A single index identifies each decision, e.g., \(x_i\). The index may be numeric, such as \(i=1,\ldots,10\) (products 1–10), or represent a set, such as \(i \in P\), where \(P=\{\text{Apple},\text{Orange},\text{Kiwi},\text{Strawberry}\}\). Variable names are also flexible—for example, \(M_i\) and \(B_i\) may denote quantities manufactured and purchased, respectively.
Multi-dimensional: Additional indices represent additional dimensions of the decision, such as facilities, products, locations, technologies, or time periods.

As more dimensions are included, the notation naturally expands. For example, if we are modeling production:

\(M_p\): quantity of product \(p\) manufactured internally.
\(M_{i,p}\): quantity of product \(p\) manufactured at facility \(i\).
\(M_{i,p,t}\): quantity of product \(p\) manufactured at facility \(i\) during time period \(t\).
\(M^{\text{int}}_{i,p}\): quantity of product \(p\) manufactured internally at facility \(i\), where the superscript distinguishes the production mode.

Here, \(i \in F\) (facilities), \(p \in P\) (products), and \(t \in T\) (time periods). In general, choose the notation that best represents the dimensions of the problem while remaining easy to interpret.

title: Linear Programming: The Foundation of Optimization
text:
2.2 Coefficients(Parameters)
Coefficients are the known constants that appear in the objective function and constraints. They describe how decision variables contribute to the objective and how they consume resources.

In the objective function, coefficients typically represent quantities such as profit and cost. They are often denoted by \(c_i\). For example, if producing one unit of product \(i\) generates $10 profit, then \(c_i = 10\).
In the constraints, coefficients represent the amount of a resource consumed or produced by a decision. For example, if producing one unit of product \(i\) requires 2 hours of labor, then the corresponding coefficient in the labor constraint is 2.

A key assumption in linear programming is that these coefficients are known with certainty. In practice, however, they may change due to uncertainty or changing conditions. The impact of changes in the coefficients can be studied using sensitivity analysis, which will be discussed later.

title: Linear Programming: The Foundation of Optimization
text:
3.3 Objective Function
In a linear programming model, the objective is either maximization or minimization. For example:

Maximize something desirable, such as profit, revenue, production output, or customer satisfaction points.
Minimize something undesirable, such as cost, emissions, waste, or transportation distance.

If there are multiple objectives that we would like to optimize simultaneously, we might turn to goal programming, which can be viewed as an extension of linear programming designed to handle multiple objectives.

Examples of Linear Objective Functions
The objective function can either maximize a desirable quantity (e.g., profit or revenue) or minimize an undesirable quantity (e.g., cost, time, emissions, or risk).
Profit maximization
\[
\max z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i x_i
\]
where \(p_i\) is the profit earned per unit of decision variable \(x_i\).
Cost minimization
\[
\min z = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
where \(c_{ij}\) is the unit transportation cost from source \(i\) to destination \(j\).
Emission minimization
\[
\min z = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{t=1}^{T} e_{ijt}x_{ijt}
\]
where \(e_{ijt}\) is the emissions associated with decision \(x_{ijt}\) during time period \(t\).
Although the notation varies across applications, every linear objective function follows the same structure:
\[
\text{Objective}=\sum (\text{coefficient} \times \text{decision variable})
\]
The coefficients represent the contribution of each decision to the objective (e.g., profit, cost, or emissions), while the optimization model chooses the decision variables to maximize or minimize the total.

title: Linear Programming: The Foundation of Optimization
text:
3.4 Constraints
Constraints represent limitations on our decisions. They define what solutions are feasible and what solutions are not. In a linear programming model, constraints are typically written using the relationships \(\leq\), \(\geq\), or \(=\).
Constraints can involve continuous, integer, or binary decision variables. If all decision variables are required to take integer values, the problem becomes an Integer Programming (IP) problem. If some decision variables are integer while others are continuous, the problem becomes a Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) problem.

Examples of Constraints
Some common examples include:

Capacity constraints: A factory may not be able to produce more than 100 units, so we write \(x_1 + x_2 \leq 100\).
Demand constraints: A customer may require at least 50 units of product, so we write \(x_1 + x_2 \geq 50\).
Balance constraints: Material entering a process must equal material leaving the process, so we write \(x_1 + x_2 = 75\).
Non-negativity constraints: Production quantities cannot be negative, so we write \(x_i \geq 0\).

Constraints can involve continuous, integer, or binary decision variables.

If all decision variables are required to take integer values, the problem becomes an Integer Programming (IP) problem.
If some decision variables are integer while others are continuous, the problem becomes a Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) problem.

title: Linear Programming: The Foundation of Optimization
text:
Matrix Form
Although optimization models are often written using summation notation, many algorithms use a compact matrix representation.
A linear programming model can be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\max \; & c^T x \\
\text{s.t.}\; & Ax \le b, \\
& x \ge 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
or equivalently as a minimization problem.
Here,

\(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is the coefficient matrix,
\(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) is the vector of decision variables,
\(b \in \mathbb{R}^{m}\) is the vector of constraint constants,
\(c \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) is the vector of objective coefficients.

This compact notation can represent optimization models containing thousands or even millions of decision variables and constraints.

Objective Function
The matrix expression
\[
c^Tx
\]
is simply the dot product of the coefficient vector and decision-variable vector:
\[
c^Tx
=
c_1x_1+c_2x_2+\cdots+c_nx_n.
\]
Even if the original decision variables are indexed (e.g., \(x_{ij}\) or \(x_{ijt}\)), they can always be rearranged into a single vector without changing the mathematical model.


Constraints
A single linear constraint has the form
\[
a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n
\le,\;=,\;\text{or}\;\ge
b.
\]
With multiple constraints, we simply stack them together:
\[
Ax \le b,\qquad
Ax=b,\qquad
\text{or}\qquad
Ax\ge b.
\]
The matrix multiplication is valid because
\[
(m\times n)(n\times1)=(m\times1),
\]
producing one equation for each constraint.

title: Simplex Method
text:
The simplex method works because linear programming has a special geometric property.
Consider:
\[
\max z=5x_1+4x_2+3x_3
\]
subject to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2x_1+3x_2+x_3 &\le5\\
4x_1+x_2+2x_3 &\le11\\
3x_1+4x_2+2x_3 &\le8\\
x_1,x_2,x_3&\ge0
\end{aligned}
\]
The constraints define a feasible region.
Every point inside this region satisfies all constraints.
The fundamental theorem of linear programming states:

If an optimal solution exists, at least one optimal solution occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region.

Therefore, simplex does not need to search every possible point.
Instead, it searches through the vertices.
The question becomes:

How can we efficiently move from one vertex to another?

The answer comes from linear algebra.

title: Simplex Method
text:
Which Variable Should Increase Next?
The objective function is still:
\[
z=5x_1+4x_2+3x_3
\]
At the current solution, \(x_1\) is already being used.
The remaining variables that can increase are:
\[
x_2,\qquad x_3
\]
Their contributions to the objective are:

Increasing \(x_2\) improves the objective by \(4\).
Increasing \(x_3\) improves the objective by \(3\).

Therefore, simplex chooses:
\[
\boxed{x_2\text{ enters the solution}}
\]
because it provides the larger improvement.

title: Simplex Method
text:
How Far Can We Increase \(x_2\)?
Now we increase \(x_2\) while keeping:
\[
x_1=2.5,\qquad x_3=0
\]
Substitute into the constraints.
The first constraint becomes:
\[
2(2.5)+3x_2\le5
\]
which gives:
\[
5+3x_2\le5
\]
so:
\[
x_2\le0
\]
This means \(x_2\) cannot increase because the first constraint is already completely used.
The second constraint gives:
\[
4(2.5)+x_2\le11
\]
so:
\[
10+x_2\le11
\]
and:
\[
x_2\le1
\]
The third constraint gives:
\[
3(2.5)+4x_2\le8
\]
so:
\[
7.5+4x_2\le8
\]
and:
\[
x_2\le0.125
\]
The smallest allowable value is:
\[
x_2=0
\]
Therefore, \(x_2\) cannot enter the solution.
This tells us something important:
The current vertex is blocked in the \(x_2\) direction because the first constraint is already tight.

title: Simplex Method
text:
Try the Remaining Direction
Now test \(x_3\).
Keep:
\[
x_1=2.5,\qquad x_2=0
\]
The constraints become:
\[
2(2.5)+x_3\le5
\]
\[
4(2.5)+2x_3\le11
\]
\[
3(2.5)+2x_3\le8
\]
The first constraint gives:
\[
5+x_3\le5
\]
so:
\[
x_3\le0
\]
Again, \(x_3\) cannot increase.
Therefore, from this vertex, no variable can improve the objective value.
The simplex method stops.
The current solution is optimal:
\[
\boxed{
x_1=2.5,\quad x_2=0,\quad x_3=0
}
\]
with:
\[
\boxed{
z=12.5
}
\]

title: Simplex Method
text:
What Did Simplex Do?
The entire process was:

Start at:

\[
(0,0,0)
\]

Choose \(x_1\) because it gives the largest objective improvement.
Increase \(x_1\) until:

\[
s_1=0
\]

Move to:

\[
(2.5,0,0)
\]

Check whether another variable can improve the objective.
Since no variable can improve the solution, stop.

The simplex method therefore finds the optimal solution by repeatedly moving:
\[
\boxed{
\text{vertex}\rightarrow\text{vertex}\rightarrow\text{vertex}
}
\]
until reaching the best possible corner.

title: Simplex Method
text:
Example of Infeasibility
Consider:
\[
\max z=x
\]
subject to:
\[
x\le2
\]
and:
\[
x\ge5
\]
The first constraint says:
\[
x\in(-\infty,2]
\]
while the second says:
\[
x\in[5,\infty)
\]
There is no overlap:
\[
(-\infty,2]\cap[5,\infty)=\emptyset
\]
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{\text{No feasible solution exists}}
\]

title: Simplex Method
text:
Example of an Unbounded Problem
Consider:
\[
\max z=x_1+x_2
\]
subject to:
\[
x_1-x_2\le2
\]
and:
\[
x_1,x_2\ge0
\]
The feasible region exists.
For example:
\[
(x_1,x_2)=(1,0)
\]
satisfies the constraint.
However, we can increase both variables:
\[
x_1=t+2
\]
and:
\[
x_2=t
\]
where:
\[
t\ge0
\]
The constraint becomes:
\[
(t+2)-t=2
\]
so it remains feasible.
The objective becomes:
\[
z=(t+2)+t
\]
which simplifies to:
\[
z=2t+2
\]
As:
\[
t\rightarrow\infty
\]
we get:
\[
z\rightarrow\infty
\]
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{\text{The problem is unbounded}}
\]

text:
1.1 Example of a Make or Buy Question
A steel manufacturer plans to transition part of its production to hydrogen-based Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) technology and requires 12,000 kg of hydrogen per day. The company already operates hydrogen production facilities and has established supply contracts with external vendors. The decision is therefore limited to determining the quantity of each hydrogen type to produce internally and purchase externally.
Three hydrogen pathways are available: green hydrogen, blue hydrogen, and grey hydrogen. The cost of producing hydrogen internally is $5.00/kg for green hydrogen, $3.50/kg for blue hydrogen, and $2.00/kg for grey hydrogen. Alternatively, hydrogen can be purchased from external suppliers at $5.50/kg, $4.00/kg, and $2.50/kg, respectively. The carbon intensities of green, blue, and grey hydrogen are 0.5, 3.0, and 9.0 kg CO₂ per kg H₂, respectively.
To support the company’s decarbonization goals, at least 10% of total hydrogen demand must be supplied by green hydrogen. Furthermore, the average carbon intensity of the hydrogen portfolio must not exceed 3.5 kg CO₂ per kg H₂. The company’s internal production facilities can supply at most 6,000 kg of hydrogen per day. External suppliers can provide at most 8,000 kg per day in total. In addition, supplier contracts limit purchases of green, blue, and grey hydrogen to 2,000 kg, 4,000 kg, and 5,000 kg per day, respectively.
Formulate a linear programming model to determine how much green, blue, and grey hydrogen should be produced internally and how much should be purchased externally in order to minimize total daily hydrogen procurement cost while satisfying all demand, environmental, production, and supply constraints.

title: What Is Linear Programming Used For? Common Applications and Examples （1）
text:
The Defining Characteristic: Mass Balance
The heart of every blending problem is the mass balance principle. In a classical mixing problem:
\[\text{Total ingredients in} = \text{Total blended product out}\]
Every unit of every ingredient needs to be accounted for. Nothing appears from nowhere; nothing disappears. If you pour 200 liters of beer, 50 liters of syrup, and 150 liters of water into a vat, you get exactly 400 liters of blended drink.
This gives rise to the fundamental blending constraint:
\[\sum_{i} x_{ij} = q_j \quad \forall j\]
where \(x_{ij}\) is the quantity of ingredient \(i\) used in product \(j\), and \(q_j\) is the total quantity of product \(j\) produced.
But in practice, ingredients usually evaporate, spill, shrink, or get consumed in chemical reactions during processing. The mass balance still holds but it simply expands to include losses as an explicit term:
\[\text{Total ingredients in} = \text{Total blended product out} + \text{Losses}\]
In LP terms, a yield factor \(\lambda_i \in (0, 1]\) captures how much of ingredient \(i\) actually makes it into the final product. The blending constraint becomes:
\[\sum_{i} \lambda_i \, x_{ij} = q_j \quad \forall j\]
When \(\lambda_i = 1\), the ingredient transfers perfectly with no loss. When \(\lambda_i = 0.95\), 5% evaporates during mixing and only 95% of what you pour in ends up in the final blend.

text:
The Second Characteristic: Quality Attributes
Beyond mass balance, each ingredient carries one or more quality attributes that propagate into the final mixture:

Quality blends proportionally — a critical assumption. If Ingredient A has 8% alcohol and Ingredient B has 0% alcohol, a 50/50 blend yields exactly 4% alcohol. This linear mixing rule is what keeps the blending problem tractable as a linear program.
The quality constraint for a minimum threshold \(\theta\) on attribute \(\alpha\) takes the form:
\[\frac{\sum_{i} \alpha_i \, x_{ij}}{q_j} \geq \theta_j \quad \forall j\]
or equivalently in linearised form:
\[\sum_{i} \alpha_i \, x_{ij} \geq \theta_j \cdot q_j \quad \forall j\]
